narrative:
The model predicted a 68% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the 2nd decile, a noticeably weaker performance in the later stage of your studies. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though with less force. You finished in the 5th decile compared with an average of 6th among accepted students, adding further concern about consistent academic performance.

Fortunately, your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 40, it sits above the 37.2 average of accepted applicants and pulled the prediction toward success. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender, race, family income, undergraduate GPA, or planned full-time status in reaching this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue further study, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score even higher. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (248 words)
